$comment: THE SPINE. Every language fills the same slots, in the same order, with the same meaning.
This file is what makes LangKraft one app rather than twenty phrasebooks. Before it existed,
each language was selected independently from its own Wikivoyage page in page order, so no
two languages shared a single Tier 0 phrase: 376 distinct English captions across 1,050
entries, and ZERO captions present in all twenty. A traveller who learned 'thank you' in
Japanese could not find 'thank you' in Thai, because nothing tied the two together.
HOW A SLOT IS DEFINED
id         stable, never reused. Format: <group>.<meaning>.
english    ONE fixed wording. This is what the app shows in EVERY language, so the tier is
navigable by a reader who has read another language's copy of the same tier.
It is not 'the English of this language's phrase' — it is the meaning, and every
language supplies a phrase for it.
concept    existing concept id, unchanged, so the evidence model and the domain caps keep
working.
domain     1-12, unchanged.
direction  say = something you produce. understand = something you receive.
match      the page captions that identify a harvested row as filling this slot. Matching
is EXPLICIT and case/punctuation-insensitive — no fuzzy matching, no scoring. An
assignment that cannot be read and checked is an assignment nobody can correct,
and an unmatched slot is reported as a gap rather than filled by the nearest
thing.
why        why this slot is in the courtesy floor. Renders verbatim in the app.
SLOTS ARE MEANINGS, NOT UTTERANCES
The pre-spine English Tier 0 carried four separate 'sorry' phrases and two 'thank you'
phrases. Transliterating that into twenty languages would mean eighty slots to fill before
anyone could ask for the price of a bus ticket. Near-synonyms collapse here: one slot per
meaning, and the register is a property of the language's phrase, not of the slot.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT
No numbers, no prices, no directions. Those are Tier 1. A courtesy floor that already
contains them stops being a floor, and the per-language sizes already show the pressure —
Thai reached 77 entries and Hindi 2, from the same declared 50.
name: Courtesy
intent: Not rude. Greet, thank, apologise, say you are learning the language, and recover from not understanding.

slots.why: The default greeting anywhere. Works with every age and every status.
Used until roughly midday. Getting the time of day wrong is noticed; not saying it is only noticed by someone expecting it.
The middle of the day. In several languages this is the same word as the evening greeting, and using it late is not an error.
From late afternoon. Often interchangeable with the afternoon greeting.
The opening move in almost every conversation. In most of these languages it is a greeting rather than a question and does not expect a literal answer.

match: i'm well, thank you. and you?
i am well, thank you. and you?
i'm well thank you and you
slots.why: The expected answer to the greeting above. Answering it wrong reads as evasive in cultures where it is a formula.
slots.match_note: WIDENED after measuring the English floor against the slot rather than from memory. The English floor's answer is the full sentence 'I'm well, thank you. And you?' rather than the fragment 'I'm well, thank you', so the exact fragment never matched. Both are listed because the phrasebooks write both forms.

slots.why: Said on a first introduction. In several languages there is a separate phrase for meeting someone formally that a stranger will use instead.
Half of every introduction. Used immediately after the greeting, with no pause between.
You get asked this before you get to ask it. Recognising the question is the difference between answering and freezing.
The question after your name, and the answer to it. Where you are from changes how you are treated, so it gets asked early.

match: this is my first time here
slots.why: Sets the whole interaction. Said once, early, it buys patience you would otherwise have to spend on being incomprehensible — and it is the difference between being ignored and being helped.
slots.caution: In several of these languages there is a separate, more formal phrase for a learner talking to an elder or an official. The neutral one can read as flippancy in a formal setting.

slots.why: Not a filler in English, and a grammatical particle in some of these languages — one word that changes a sentence from an order to a request.
The single most useful word in any of these languages. Saying it costs nothing and changes how everything after it is received.
You will be handed it constantly, and there is no way to avoid replying. In a few languages the reply is the same word as 'yes'.

match: excuse me (getting attention of server, speaker is male)
excuse me (getting attention of server, speaker is female)
slots.why: Two different things in one phrase: getting someone's attention, and getting past them. Guessing wrong is jarring — one version walks through a conversation.

match: sorry, could you say that again?
slots.why: Apologising for a small fault — bumping someone, being late, not understanding. The form you use signals how much of a fault you think it was.
Buys you time to think, find a word, or finish what you were doing — without the silence that reads as rude or as not understanding.
Held doors with it. Skipping it is marked in cultures where order and seniority are visible in everyday speech.
How you leave. Leaving without one is noticeably rude in most of these languages.
The longer goodbye, and the one that implies you may meet again. Usually follows the first goodbye rather than replacing it.

match: i don't know what you mean
i don't know what that means
slots.why: The one phrase that keeps a conversation alive. Without it people stop trying, and with it they often rephrase in simpler words.

match: could you speak more slowly, please?
could you say that again, please?
slots.why: Asks for the thing you actually need. Saying it is nearly always received well, even badly pronounced, and asking again is not.
slots.match_note: WIDENED after measuring the English floor against the slot rather than from memory. Same shape: the English floor writes 'Could you speak more slowly, please?' and the list held only the shorter form. Both are listed.

match: i can't hear you (or understand you)
slots.why: Distinguishes not hearing from not understanding, because they have different fixes and conflating them produces the wrong one.
How you learn a word instead of nodding. Asking is how a phrasebook gets used instead of recited.
slots.match_note: WIDENED after measuring the corpus: the first list was exact captions and matched nothing. The meaning is identical across the pages that have it; only the language name or phrasing differs.

slots.why: For words you heard used rather than shown, which is most of them.

match: can you help me with this
could you help me with this
slots.why: The opener for every request that follows. Standing in front of someone not being asked anything is how people get ignored.
The honest answer, and in some cultures the only acceptable one — guessing when you don't know reads as deceit rather than as effort.
Closes a transaction. Used to shops, to waiters, and to anyone who has finished and is waiting for you to leave.
You get asked it after anything you say, and the honest answer is the only useful one.
Asked of you constantly, and the question that decides whether anything after it can happen. There is a polite version and a blunt version and the gap between them is wide.
The answer to the question above, and the thing that tells a speaker to switch to simpler words rather than to English.
slots.match_note: WIDENED after measuring the corpus: the first list was exact captions and matched nothing. The meaning is identical across the pages that have it; only the language name or phrasing differs.

slots.why: Saying it when you do not is worse than silence, because it removes the reason to simplify. Said when you do, it invites the harder version.

_match_patterns: An entry ending in * is a PREFIX match. Needed because some captions embed the language's own name — 'How do you say this in Thai?' — so an exact-caption list can never match more than the one page that happens to phrase it that way. Nothing else is fuzzy: every pattern is still written out by hand and readable.
